lessons.title: Fruit kinds and their features
lessons.html:
Know the fruit you handle

Every fruit kind has its own characteristics: how it looks, feels, ripens and stores. When you know these, you handle the fruit correctly and can recognise when something is wrong.

Main fruit groups in South African packhouses

GroupExamplesTypical features
CitrusOranges, soft citrus (mandarins), lemons, grapefruitThick peel with oil glands; does not ripen further after picking
Pome fruitApples, pearsFirm flesh, core with seeds; many ripen after picking; can store for months
Stone fruitPeaches, nectarines, plums, apricots, cherriesOne hard stone; soft skin, bruises easily; short storage life
Table grapesWhite, red and black cultivarsBunches; berries can fall off (shatter); stems dry out quickly
SubtropicalAvocados, mangoes, litchisSensitive to cold injury; many ripen after picking

Characteristics we look at

  • Size and shape: typical for the cultivar.
  • Colour: background colour and blush; shows maturity.
  • Firmness: how hard the fruit is.
  • Skin or peel: smooth, rough, waxy, thin or thick.
  • Taste: sugar (sweetness) and acid (sourness).
  • Juice content: important for citrus.
  • Aroma: smell of ripe fruit.

Cultivars

Within one kind there are many cultivars, for example Navel and Valencia oranges, Granny Smith and Royal Gala apples, Packham's Triumph and Forelle pears. Cultivars differ in colour, shape, season and how they must be handled. Never mix cultivars in a carton.

Even within one cultivar, fruit from different orchards or picked on different days can behave differently. That is why fruit is kept in batches by producer and orchard, and why quality controllers test samples from each batch.

lessons.title: Maturity, ripening and keeping quality
lessons.html:
Mature and ripe are not the same

A fruit is mature when it has developed enough on the tree to ripen properly and taste good later. A fruit is ripe when it is ready to eat. Export fruit is picked mature but often not yet fully ripe, so it can survive the long journey.

How maturity is measured

  • Colour charts compare the fruit's colour to standard pictures.
  • Firmness is measured with a penetrometer (pressure tester).
  • Sugar content (total soluble solids, TSS) is measured with a refractometer, in degrees Brix.
  • Acid and the sugar-acid ratio, important for citrus.
  • Starch in apples and pears, shown with an iodine test.
  • Juice percentage in citrus.

Markets set minimum standards for these. The quality controller tests samples before and during packing.

Ripening and ethylene

Some fruits, called climacteric fruits (apples, pears, stone fruit, avocados, mangoes), keep ripening after picking and give off a gas called ethylene, which speeds up ripening. Others, called non-climacteric (citrus, grapes, cherries), do not ripen further after picking; they only age. This is why some fruits must not be stored together.

What shortens keeping quality

CauseEffect
HeatFaster ripening, softening and decay
Bruising and cutsBrown spots and entry points for rot
Water lossShrivelling and dry stems
Wrong cold temperatureChilling injury in sensitive fruit
Decay organismsMoulds and rots spreading in the carton

Your role

Handle gently, keep fruit cool and shaded, keep cultivars apart, and report fruit that looks over-ripe, soft, shrivelled or rotten.

Key points

  • Each fruit group has its own features, such as citrus, pome, stone fruit and grapes.
  • Characteristics include size, colour, firmness, skin, taste and juice.
  • Mature means ready to ripen; ripe means ready to eat.
  • Maturity is measured with colour charts, penetrometers and refractometers.
  • Heat, bruising and water loss shorten keeping quality.
